Song Sources

The notes for the classical pieces, hymns and folk songs are taken from the MIDI and score files of Mutopia Project, Open Hymnal Project and Wikimedia Commons (licenses are shown in the table below, as stated by the original authors). “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star” and the songs marked “written by hand from the original melody” in the table are melodies and accompaniments written for this game from public domain originals; the 3 songs of “Neon · Delphinus” are original works made for this game. The main melody is taken from the melody part in each file, and each song is played with instrument sounds close to the original instrumentation (see “Instrument Sounds” below).

28Canon in DPachelbelc. 1680Written by hand from the public domain original score · Public Domain
Transcribed note by note from the Violin I part on page 1 of the handwritten full score held by the Berlin State Library (c. 1838, Canon a 3 Violini con Basso), measures 3–18 (measures 1–2 are the ground bass alone, with Violin I resting, and are omitted); D major, 4/4, not transposed. The thirty-second-note variations that begin at measure 19 are not included; the ending is one added measure of our own, extending the first note of measure 19, A5, over a D chord to close. Chords follow the Cembalo ground bass D A B F# G D G A (one beat per note).
29Spring (The Four Seasons)Vivaldi1725Written by hand from the public domain original score · Public Domain
Based on the Violino Principale part of the 1739 Le Clerc edition (Gallica btv1b9062998d), page 2, “La Primavera” Allegro: the pickup plus the opening ritornello in measures 1–13, and the B section bird song in measures 13–27 (up to before the Tutti enters); E major, 4/4, not transposed, no repeats omitted. The original has only the solo part; where the other violins answer in the bird song section, the soloist rests (the rests in measures 17, 18 and 19 are kept as in the original); chords are fitted to the melody as E / A / B triads (this page has no bass part to compare against). A 3.5-beat rest is added before the pickup E5 to make a full measure; ornaments (+, m.) are omitted; after the final half-note E6, a two-beat rest is added so that the excerpt ends before the Tutti.

33Sonata K. 545Mozart1788Written by hand from the public domain original score · Public Domain
Based on the PDF of the old Breitkopf & Härtel complete edition (ed. Rudorff, Sonate Nr.15), page 200 measures 1–24 and the first line of page 201 (measures 25–28), exposition of the first movement (no repeat); the melody is the right hand, and the chords follow the left-hand Alberti bass / chord analysis; trills are not expanded (measures 4, 15, 17 and 25 write only the main note), grace notes (measures 22, 23) are omitted, and the 32nd-note turn in measure 23 is changed to 16th notes (the dotted quarter is shortened to a quarter); for chords, the top note is taken as the melody (measures 12, 28)
34Fantaisie-Impromptu (Theme)Chopin1834Mutopia Project (Chopin, Fantaisie-Impromptu Op. 66) · Public Domain / No rights reserved
35Raindrop PreludeChopin1839Mutopia Project · Public Domain · Magnus Lewis-Smith
36The Blue DanubeJohann Strauss II1867Written by hand from the public domain original score · Public Domain
Based on page 4 of C. A. Spina’s 1867 first edition piano solo score (Commons Donauwalzer_Spina_04.jpg), Walzer No.1, measures 1–32, D major, 3/4, up to the double bar line where the key changes, no repeats. The melody takes the highest voice of the right hand (the main melody alternating with octave-higher “echo” chords); in measures 28–29 the right hand is additionally doubled at the higher octave (F#6, D6), and to keep the melody continuous the lower main voice F#5, D5 is used instead; the chord in measure 32 takes only its top note; small slashed grace notes are omitted. Chords are inferred from the left-hand bass. The original marks only Tempo di Valse; the game uses ♩=132.
37Wedding MarchMendelssohn1842Written by hand from the public domain original score · Public Domain
Based on the Breitkopf & Härtel 1848 full score of “A Midsummer Night’s Dream”, No. 9 Hochzeitmarsch (PDF pages 141–142, full score page numbers 137–138). The fanfare takes the top notes of the three trumpets (in C, written pitch is sounding pitch) in measures 1–5; the theme takes the top voice of the flute / Violin I in measures 6–13, repeated once, with the first ending (1ma Volta, measures 14–17, trumpet fanfare) in between; on beat 4 of measure 13 the first time adds the trumpet triplet pickup, the second time rests instead, closing on C. For the first note of measures 6 and 10, which also has chord tones doubled at the octave, only the top note is taken; trills and grace notes are omitted; the second ending after measure 13 of the second time is not used. Chords are inferred from the bass part (Violoncello/Basso); in the fanfare section the orchestra rests, and a C chord stands in for the accompaniment. The original tempo is Allegro vivace; the game uses ♩=96.
38Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2Chopin1832Written by hand from the public domain original score · Public Domain
Based on page 6 of the PDF of the 1832 Kistner first edition: pickup + measures 1–10 (theme A, the ornamented variation of A, and the first phrase of section B, ending on the Bb4 at poco ritard.); 12/8 with the quarter note as the beat (6 beats per measure); the original prints M.M. ♩=132 (generally interpreted as the eighth note), which is slowed here to quarter note = 60; trills, turn signs and mordents are not expanded, and grace notes are omitted (measures 7, 8, 10); chords take the top note of the right hand as the melody, with the harmony based on the left-hand bass and chord analysis; some chords are simplified readings

46Carmen PreludeBizet1875Written by hand from the public domain original score · Public Domain
Based on the Choudens 1883 piano-vocal score, Prélude (PDF pages 9–11, score page numbers 1–3). The march theme is measures 1–16 of page 1 (A major, 2/4), repeated once as in the original; after that the middle section, the return of the theme and the pp transition are omitted, going straight to the Toreador Song starting at line 5 of page 2 (with an F major flavor, written with naturals on top of the A major key signature), 20 measures in all, ending on the C5 at the dim. in measure 2 of line 1 on page 3. The melody takes the top voice of the right hand, and chords take only the top note; trills, grace notes and small ornamental notes are omitted; ties across measures are merged into one long note. Chords are inferred from the left hand. The original tempo is ♩=116; the game uses ♩=96 (to keep the triplet sixteenth notes from being shorter than 0.1 seconds). (The Toreador section contains triplets, and the floating-point beat totals have a tiny error, so that section is marked free; it is actually 20 full measures.)

68Aloha ʻOeQueen Liliʻuokalanic. 1878Written by hand from the public domain original score · Public Domain
Based on the Broder & Schlam edition of “Mele Hawaii” (ed. H. Berger), song 2 Aloha Oe, PDF page 2 (piano introduction and the melody of verses 1 and 2) and page 3 (chorus for four-part choir + piano, taking the soprano melody and the piano left-hand bass). Original key B-flat major, 4/4, not transposed (melody F4–Eb5). The excerpt = the first verse (8 measures, taking the notes that go with the first verse’s lyrics) + two rounds of the chorus (the second round does not end with a pickup). No introduction is added. Measure 4 of the verse follows the original (beat 4 is a pickup of dotted eighth F4 + sixteenth Bb4). At the end of verse measure 8, when joining the chorus pickup F4, the original’s quarter rest is shortened to an eighth rest so that the bar lines line up. Chords are filled in by hand from the piano left-hand bass (Bb, Eb, F7) plus the melody harmony, with the bass of each measure following the original.

84Waltz of the FlowersTchaikovsky1892Written by hand from the melody of the public domain original (compared with the Primo part of the G. Schirmer 1918 piano four-hands edition of the “Nutcracker Suite” Op.71a, printed pages 53 and 55 (PDF pages 61 and 63); the Secondo is on printed pages 52 and 54) · Public Domain
Written by hand measure by measure from the Primo part of the Schirmer 1918 edition, D major, 3/4, tempo ♩=120 (slower than the original’s waltz tempo, to suit Normal difficulty). Section A and the first half of section B take the lower staff of the Primo (in B1 measures 6–7 and B2 measures 4–9 the melody is on the upper staff), and section C takes the upper staff; the whole piece keeps the original pitches, with no octave shifts; each section takes only one melodic line (in B1 measure 8, the lower F#, E descending line is taken, omitting the inserted upper G#, G, A); the introduction, harp cadenza, repeat signs and first ending are omitted; the quintuplet sixteenth-note turn in section C of the original is simplified to three notes per beat; measures 1–3 of section E are taken from the second ending, and measure 4 is a transition of our own; the ending of A3 is our own ending, closing on the tonic D. The accompaniment chords are our own (referring to the Secondo bass, with some replaced by similar triads and seventh chords).

93Flight of the BumblebeeRimsky-Korsakov1900Written by hand from the public domain original score · Public Domain
Based on the Bessel c. 1900–01 piano reduction of “The Tale of Tsar Saltan” (Rimsky-Korsakov died in 1908), Act 3 Scene 1 “Flight of the Bumblebee”, PDF pages 114–115 (printed pages 108–109), from rehearsal number 156 Vivace, the right-hand chromatic sixteenth notes, 22 measures in all (2/4, up to the measure before rehearsal number 157), no repeats. The original is marked Vivace ♩=144; the game slows it to ♩=62 and keeps all the sixteenth notes; at the ending, the A4–A3–A3–A3 on beat 1 of rehearsal number 157 is changed to a long A4 to close. Chords follow the original’s left-hand harmony on each beat (E7, Am, D, Dm, A7, G, Gm), and the accompaniment figure is our own.
94Toccata in D MinorJ. S. Bachc. 1708Mutopia Project · Public Domain · Anonymous
Takes the opening toccata section, closing on a D minor cadence chord. Checked against volume 15 of the Bach-Gesellschaft complete edition (printed by Breitkopf & Härtel): one wrong note in measure 23 is corrected (B-flat changed to E), and the melody notes in three places that had been put on the accompaniment track are restored to the melody.
95La CampanellaLiszt1851Wikimedia Commons Public Domain score: Liszt, “Grandes études de Paganini”, No. 3 “The Bell”, Breitkopf & Härtel c. 1851 edition (Internet Archive b10312122 scan); pitches were located by image recognition of the notehead positions and then checked by hand measure by measure, and compared against another scan of the same edition (Internet Archive b10271399) · Public Domain · Wikimedia Commons Public Domain score (Breitkopf & Härtel original edition scan)
G-sharp minor, 6/8, 12 sixteenth notes per measure. Takes the theme section of measures 6–20 of the original (starting from “ben marcato il tema”), played twice, with melody notes alternating with the high D# bell tone; the 8va marks in the original are intermittent (under 8va are measure 6 to the first 4 sixteenth notes of measure 7, the second half of measure 9 to the first 4 sixteenth notes of measure 11, the whole of measure 12, the 3rd sixteenth note of measure 13 to the first 6 sixteenth notes of measure 15, and the second half of measure 17 to measure 20). Here, the 8va passages use the written pitch (that is, the actual pitch after lowering the whole piece by one octave), and the passages not under 8va are lowered a further 12 semitones, so that the relative octaves of the sections match the original piece, with the bell falling within D#6; the introduction (measures 1–5) and grace notes (small notes) are omitted, and the double sharp F## is written as the same-sounding G; in the double note on the 11th sixteenth note of measure 11 (written D#5/C#5), only C#5 is taken (C#4 after lowering by an octave); the ending takes the right hand’s rising arpeggio from measure 21 of the original (the closing measure), keeping the written pitch without lowering it a further octave. Accompaniment chords are our own.
96Caprice No. 24Paganini1820The theme is written by hand from Paganini’s original (published 1820, Public Domain) and compared against Wikimedia Commons “Paganini caprice24 theme.mid”; the variations are written by us following the harmony of the original · Public Domain
A minor, 2/4; plays the theme first (16 measures), then three self-composed virtuoso variations (arpeggios, octave leaps, scales), closing on the tonic.

Art

The game’s background images (ai_*.webp), meteor images (meteor_*.webp) and Hikari expression images (emo_*.webp) were made with the help of generative AI; all other cosmetics are drawn by code.
